artwork.title: Winged Victory of Samothrace
artwork.imageCredit: TO CHECK: needs a Public Domain or CC0 photo

lessons.title: Look down first

n1.text: A winged woman leans into the wind above you. The goddess alone is more than three metres tall, and she has no head.

b1a.text: The wings give her a huge silhouette you can read from far away. Hold that thought, though: not every feather up there is ancient.

b1b.text: The cloth clings to her front and swings out behind. Remember it: that's how the sculptor shows a wind you can't see.

b1c.text: Sharp eye. Most visitors never look down, and what's down there is the key to the whole monument.

n2.text: Look down: she stands on the prow of a stone warship. She's Nike, victory in person. The wings say she can fly; the ship says this victory has to do with the sea.

q2.text: No wind was carved. So how do you know it's blowing?

b2a.text: Exactly. Thin cloth presses against her chest and legs while a heavier mantle billows out behind. You read the wind from how the fabric reacts.

b2b.text: Partly. The wings carry the motion too. But the clearest clue is the fabric: pressed flat in front, billowing out behind.

n3.text: Cloth that clings to show the body beneath is called wet drapery. It's a sculptor's language, not proof she was splashed by the sea. Now compare the goddess with her ship.

q3.text: Are the goddess and the ship the same stone?

b3a.text: Look at the colours: a white figure, a greyer ship. The goddess is Parian marble; the ship and base come from Lartos on Rhodes.

b3b.text: Right. Parian marble for her, greyer marble from Lartos on Rhodes for the ship and base.

n4.text: She's engineering as much as carving: torso and wings made separately and assembled, the hull pieced from many blocks. She first stood high in the Sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace.

q4.text: Who paid for this victory monument?

choices.label: A king, after a famous sea battle

b4a.text: Tempting, given the ship. But which battle, and which ruler or city paid, can't be named. Even her sculptor is unknown.

b4b.text: Right. The prow points to a naval victory and the Rhodian stone to a regional link, but the battle, the sponsor and the sculptor are all unknown.

n5.text: What we do know: pilgrims and visitors came to the sanctuary, so a military victory was shown again and again in a shared sacred place. Now, about those magnificent wings.

q5.text: How much of those spread wings is ancient marble?

b5a.text: Less than it looks. She was found broken. The fully spread right wing is plaster, parts of the torso are restored, and a metal frame holds the wings.

b5b.text: Right. The right wing is a plaster replacement, parts of the torso are restored, and a metal structure holds the wings up.

n6.text: In the 19th century, researchers realised scattered grey blocks were the ship. A 2013 to 2014 restoration then reconnected goddess and ship directly. Take the ship away and she still means victory, but not where it was won.

lessons.takeaway: Look down first: the ship makes it a victory at sea. The cloth shows you the wind, and the right wing is plaster.
